## Methodology

Off-device microbenchmarks exercise engine hot paths under Bun on the developer machine — pure algorithmic cost, no Skia rasterization, no React Native bridge, no device I/O. Their value is regression detection and order-of-magnitude sizing; they do **not** predict on-device frame times. For real frame times see the [Device](#device) section.

Each capture run warms a scenario for a fixed time budget (not a fixed batch count, which warms a cheap scenario for microseconds and an expensive one for seconds, measuring the two at different JIT tiers), then times N inner iterations per sample and reports that run's median. A baseline folds several independent runs together: the published cost is the median of those per-run medians, and "Spread across runs" is their lowest and highest.

The **p99** column is populated only for rows captured with at least 100 samples. Below that a "99th percentile" is just the worst sample wearing a statistical name, so those rows show `—` and the **max** column carries the tail instead.

Captured with `__DEV__ === false` — the React Native release configuration, and the state the diagnostic counters' "cost only when armed" design assumes. It is recorded because it used to be load-bearing: until 2026-07-29 the engine read the dev flag as a bare `__DEV__` identifier behind a `typeof` guard, and JSC has no inline cache for an unresolvable global, so a capture taken with the flag *undeclared* read ~7x high on every render row and was measuring a JSC deoptimisation rather than the engine. The hot sites now read a `globalThis` property instead, so the configuration no longer changes the result — but a capture that cannot say which configuration it ran under still cannot be compared with one that can.

Frame budget at 60 fps is 16.67 ms. A system taking 1 ms per step leaves 15+ ms for the rest of the frame.

Treat a change smaller than the run-to-run spread as noise.  The render and integration suites drive the real `createFrameRenderer` pipeline against a counting Skia stub, so per-sprite transform construction — including the rotation branch — is inside the measured region.

## What these numbers do not measure

- **No Skia rasterization, no GPU, no bridge, no device.** The draw path runs to the point where the engine hands a batch to Skia; what Skia then does with it is not measured here, and these are pure JS costs under Bun on one desktop machine.
- **Web/CanvasKit numbers exist in three lanes: CPU-raster, desktop GPU, and an on-device Android GPU lane.** See [Web (CanvasKit)](#web-canvaskit). Both GPU-backed lanes measure **CPU-side submission cost**, not GPU execution time — WebGL/CanvasKit calls queue work and return, and reading true GPU time from page script is not available to this harness. Every web figure published before 2026-08-18 was quantized to the display refresh interval and must not be cited.
- **The ECS suite is deliberately unbounded.** Its entities integrate off the field forever, because nothing in `world.step` branches on position and holding that suite byte-identical across the 2026-07 rework keeps it usable as the control row that made the render regression conclusive. The physics and integration suites wrap at the field edge instead, and a probe fails the capture if any entity escapes.
- **Heap figures are a footprint proxy, not a retention measurement.** See the heap section.
- **Correction, 2026-08-19: every node figure published before this date was ~2.5x too slow.** The capture machine was running the Windows "Power saver" plan. Re-capturing the identical commit under "High performance" made **all 38 scenarios faster by 2.42x-2.58x, median 2.49x** - a band that tight across ECS, physics, particles, render and integration is a clock-rate effect, not a code one. Nothing in the harness could see it: the machine was quiet, so the load guard passed, and the spread guard passed whenever five runs happened to land in one clock state. Captures now record the active power plan in their provenance, and `bench:promote` refuses a window taken under Power saver. Balanced is warned about rather than refused - its effect has never been measured here.
- **Every number here was captured on a machine that was 5.9% busy with other work.** `bench:promote` refuses a window above 15% foreign load, or one where 2 or more runs sit further than 10% from the folded median. Both exist because two captures taken beside a fleet of agent processes once read a headline row 23% low, and nothing but a human noticed (B29).
- **`particles.update 500 integrate-only` is held to a wider tolerance than every other row (35%, not 10%), and is less reproducible than its neighbours.** Bimodal across 1.70-2.10 us (1.24x), split 12 low / 3 high over the 15 pinned captures recorded on 2026-08-20, with each state internally tight — so the folded median lands in whichever state that window caught, and moves between them. Read the spread column, not the median, for this row.
- **`particles.update 1000 integrate-only` is held to a wider tolerance than every other row (35%, not 10%), and is less reproducible than its neighbours.** Bimodal across 3.37-4.24 us (1.26x), split 14 low / 1 high over the 15 pinned captures recorded on 2026-08-20, with each state internally tight — so the folded median lands in whichever state that window caught, and moves between them. Read the spread column, not the median, for this row.
- **`particles.update 2000 integrate-only` is held to a wider tolerance than every other row (35%, not 10%), and is less reproducible than its neighbours.** Bimodal across 6.73-8.85 us (1.32x), split 7 low / 8 high over the 15 pinned captures recorded on 2026-08-20, with each state internally tight — so the folded median lands in whichever state that window caught, and moves between them. Read the spread column, not the median, for this row.
- **`particles.update 5000 integrate-only` is held to a wider tolerance than every other row (35%, not 10%), and is less reproducible than its neighbours.** Bimodal across 16.80-21.40 us (1.27x), split 9 low / 6 high over the 15 pinned captures recorded on 2026-08-20, with each state internally tight — so the folded median lands in whichever state that window caught, and moves between them. Read the spread column, not the median, for this row.
- **The table cannot show the 2026-07-29 dev-flag fix, because the bench has always declared `__DEV__`.** Until that date the engine read the flag as a bare identifier behind a `typeof` guard, once per sprite per transform pass. Under **JSC** — Bun, and Safari/iOS WebKit — an unresolvable global costs ~270 ns per evaluation, so a consumer who never defines `__DEV__` was paying it: `render.flush 1000 / 1 atlas` measured 412-450 µs in that configuration against 56-88 µs after the fix, the same band the declared configuration occupies. React Native always defines the flag and was never affected. **V8 (Node, Chrome) and SpiderMonkey were never measured** — the ~270 ns figure is JSC-only and must not be read as a cross-engine claim.

## Draw-path allocation counters

Exact integers, not timings: every row runs the real frame renderer against an injected Skia stub that counts each object it is asked to build, and reads the engine's own pool counters. In steady state the sprite-command pool must miss zero times, the particle pool must call its factory zero times, and the renderer must ask Skia for zero new objects — every rect, transform and paint it needs is already pooled. "Skia calls / frame" counts the calls the renderer repeats every frame **by design** (a colour filter or shader is rebuilt per draw call); those are a property of the effect, not a leak.

These counters cannot see allocations that pass through neither a pool nor the injected factory — the cached slices in `frame-renderer.ts` are the known example — which is why the isolated heap probe below stays as the whole-heap backstop.

## Integration heap

Each scenario runs in its **own process**, warms up until two consecutive block deltas fall under the instrument's resolution (so the heap has reached the plateau its allocation rate implies), then reports the median per-frame delta across 3 measured blocks of 200 / 100 / 50 frames — block length scales with entity count so every scenario measures a comparable amount of allocation work — with forced GCs at every boundary.

Read this as an allocation-pressure proxy, not as retention. Under JSC `process.memoryUsage().heapUsed` reports MarkedSpace block footprint rather than live bytes, so it moves with GC scheduling and with how far the heap has climbed toward its plateau. The previous instrument measured 30 warm-up frames and one forced GC in a process that had already run every other suite, and published the resulting climb as "+15.7 / +33.4 / +31.1 KB per frame retained growth"; re-measured after a full warm-up the same scenarios read between -0.2 and +2.5 KB/frame, with every structural counter flat. Retention claims belong to the exact counters above.

## Web (CanvasKit)

Three lanes over the same 18 render scenarios (frozen in `scenario-contract.ts`), bound to real CanvasKit through `@flare-engine/render-web` instead of the node lane's counting Skia stub: **CPU-raster** renders through an offscreen `CanvasKit.MakeSurface`, CPU-backed by construction, which is the driver-independent baseline a CI runner can also produce; **GPU** renders through a real on-screen `<canvas>` + WebGL surface on this desktop; **Android device** runs that same on-screen path on a USB-attached phone. Every record carries `runtime: "web-cpu-raster"`, `"web-gpu"` or `"web-android-gpu"`, never a bare `"web"`, and each lane writes its own results and history files, so they can never be folded into one series.

> **Measurement correction, 2026-08-18 — every web number published before this date was wrong.** The original sampler ran the work once per `requestAnimationFrame` callback and took the frame-to-frame delta as its sample. rAF is vsync-locked, so that delta can only ever be an integer multiple of the display refresh interval, which made every reported figure `k x 16.667 ms / innerIters` for integer `k`. All 36 rows across both lanes were such multiples. **13 of the 18 GPU rows sat at exactly k = 1** — they reported the display's refresh rate and nothing whatsoever about the engine. Work cheaper than one refresh interval was invisible to that clock by construction. The sampler now brackets the work with `performance.now()` and uses rAF only to schedule batches, and grows each batch until it fills a ~20 ms window — long enough that Chrome's 100 us Spectre clamp on `performance.now()` is noise — instead of running a fixed `innerIters` count that was sized for the node bench against a counting stub. Every lane below was captured on the corrected instrument. **Nothing below is comparable to a web capture published before 2026-08-18.**

**Both GPU lanes measure CPU-side submission cost, not GPU execution time.** WebGL and CanvasKit calls queue work and return — `GrDirectContext.flush()` submits, it does not wait — so a clock bracket captures everything the CPU does to build and hand off the frame and none of what the GPU then does with it. Reading true GPU time from page script needs `EXT_disjoint_timer_query_webgl2` (generally not exposed) or a forced `finish()`/`readPixels` sync, which distorts the number by serializing the pipeline. Submission cost is in any case the figure a consumer's frame budget contends with on the main thread.

The **Ops/batch** column is the honesty check: it is how many repetitions filled the measurement window, so `p50 x ops` reconstructs that window. A row whose `p50` equals `refresh / ops` is the failure mode described above, and this column makes it visible rather than invisible.

Sources: `web.json` / `web-gpu.json` / `web-android.json` (folded baseline per lane) with matching `*-history.ndjson` files, each lane kept separate from the node lane's `history.ndjson` so its rows can never land inside `bench:promote`'s blind `rows.slice(-N)` window. Capture with `bun run bench:web`, `bench:web:gpu` or `bench:web:android` in `apps/bench-web`, then fold with `bun run bench:web:promote -- --lane <lane> --runs N` in `benchmarks`. **Every figure below is a median-of-medians across the runs stated in its header, with the observed spread beside it** — the fold refuses a window whose captures disagree on commit, runtime, browser, renderer or phone, one the device was thermally throttling through, or one where two or more runs sit more than 10% from the folded median.

### CanvasKit WASM payload

Read straight off the installed `canvaskit-wasm` package on disk (raw = file size, gzip = `gzip -c <file> | wc -c`) — never hardcoded.

| Variant | Raw | Gzipped |
|---|---:|---:|
| default | 7,094,511 B (6.77 MB) | 2,852,025 B (2.72 MB) |
| full | 8,001,100 B (7.63 MB) | 3,200,682 B (3.05 MB) |

`apps/bench-web` serves the `full` binary (needed for the render suite's effect coverage); `default` is the smaller number a production integration that skips those features would ship.

### Cold start to first rendered frame

"First rendered frame" = the first `surface.flush()` after CanvasKit finishes loading, on the off-screen CPU-raster surface the render suite itself uses — there is no on-screen `<canvas>` here, so browser paint/composite timings (FCP etc.) do not apply.

| Cache | Plain network | Throttled 4G |
|---|---:|---:|
| cold | 58.0 ms | 16.32 s |
| warm | 35.9 ms | 16.31 s |

4G throttle profile (Chrome DevTools Protocol `Network.emulateNetworkConditions`, a flare-engine-defined profile stated here for reproducibility — not a copy of any external tool's preset): **download 4 Mbit/s (524288 B/s), upload 3 Mbit/s (393216 B/s), latency 20 ms**.

The throttled cold/warm pair reads nearly identical. Measured directly (via CDP `Network.responseReceived.fromDiskCache`) that headless Chromium does not serve this WASM fetch from its HTTP disk cache in this harness — true even for two back-to-back same-page fetches with no navigation at all, despite a `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable` response header — so both throttled rows pay the full download. Read that as a property of this headless measurement harness, not as "repeat visits get no benefit on a real 4G connection"; the untouched pair's warm speedup (from V8's WASM compile cache and local file-read caching, not HTTP caching) is the more representative signal.

### Render suite — desktop GPU

_Captured: 2026-09-05 · Median of 5 run(s) · Commit: e6a3919a4cbe · Runtime: web-gpu · Host: win32 x64 (13th Gen Intel(R) Core(TM) i9-13900KF) · Engine version: 0.3.1 · Browser: chromium 151.0.7922.34 · Renderer: `ANGLE (NVIDIA, NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4070 Ti (0x00002782) Direct3D11 vs_5_0 ps_5_0, D3D11)`_

Headless Chromium does **not** default to hardware acceleration — with no GPU-related launch flags it silently reports SwiftShader for `UNMASKED_RENDERER_WEBGL` even without `--disable-gpu` — so `playwright.config.ts` pins `--use-angle=d3d11` for this mode, and `browser-driver.mjs` refuses to write a result whose reported renderer still matches `/swiftshader/i`. The renderer string above (`WEBGL_debug_renderer_info`) is the proof this capture used the host GPU.

`render.flush 1000 sprites / 1 atlas` costs **0.126 ms** submitting on the GPU path against **11.300 ms** rasterizing on the CPU path — a factor of **90x** on this one desktop machine. Read that as "CanvasKit's software rasterizer is enormously more expensive than handing the same frame to a GPU driver", not as a figure that generalizes to other hardware or to a mobile GPU.

The three `render.sort` rows touch neither surface — pure JS array sorting — and read close to one another across both lanes, as expected. **Under the old sampler they read *identically*, and an earlier version of this document credited that to the shared code path. The real cause was that both lanes pinned those rows to the vsync floor.** Freed of it they differ slightly, which is ordinary run-to-run variation on identical work.

### Render suite — Android device (on-device GPU)

_Captured: 2026-08-27 · Median of 5 run(s) · Commit: 6549fa207ce8 · Runtime: web-android-gpu · Device: Pixel 7 (panther, GS201, Android 17) · Engine version: 0.3.0 · Browser: chrome-android 151.0.7922.173 · Renderer: `ANGLE (ARM, Mali-G710, OpenGL ES 3.2)`_

The same 18 scenarios on real phone hardware, through the identical on-screen `<canvas>` + WebGL path as the desktop GPU lane, so the submission-cost caveat above applies here too.

`bun run bench:web:android` starts the bench server on the host, opens `adb reverse tcp:<port> tcp:<port>` so `localhost:<port>` on the phone resolves back to it, then attaches to the phone's Chrome over its `@chrome_devtools_remote` socket via `adb forward` + `connectOverCDP`. Chrome is **attached to, never launched** — `playwright._android`'s `launchBrowser()` hangs against retail Chrome on this device, and the browser belongs to whoever is holding the phone. The driver refuses to write a capture whose `UNMASKED_RENDERER_WEBGL` reads as a software rasterizer, the same guard the desktop GPU lane uses. Hardware identity comes from `getprop` at capture time, so a row names the phone it actually ran on. Requirements: exactly one authorised device in `adb devices` (the lane refuses zero and refuses to guess between several), USB debugging accepted, screen unlocked throughout.

The phone costs **2.7x-4.8x** of the desktop's submission time on the flush scenarios and **2.0x-2.5x** on `render.sort`. That split is the informative part: `render.sort` is pure JS with no surface involved, so it isolates raw single-thread JS throughput, where this SoC lands close to a desktop i9. The flush rows add real driver and GPU-submission work, and that is where the gap widens. Neither figure is a frame-rate prediction — it is main-thread cost per operation, which is what a frame budget on this device actually contends with.

Caveat on repeatability: the phone is thermally and governor-managed in ways the desktop is not. The fold reads Android's own throttling state (`dumpsys thermalservice`) either side of every capture and **refuses any window in which the device reported throttling**, or in which the status was not reported at all — unrecorded is not the same claim as not-throttling. Battery temperature is recorded beside it (23.4 -> 25.7 C across the five folded runs) but deliberately **not** gated: no throttled capture has ever been measured with this instrument, so any drift threshold would be invented rather than calibrated. Nothing here pins the CPU/GPU governor.

## Notes on interpretation

- **ECS** — "op" is one `world.step(dt)` running the move system over all entities. Per-entity cost = `cost / entities`.
- **Physics** — "op" is one frame: move every collider (wrapping at the field edge) + `world.step()`. "dense" packs colliders into a 500×500 area (many overlaps); "sparse" uses 2000×2000 (few). Density is now held constant for the whole sample window.
- **Particles** — "integrate-only" holds N particles alive and calls `update(dt)` — measures pool integration cost. "emit+integrate" runs a saturated emitter at 2× cap/s with gravity.
- **Render** — `flush` queues N sprite commands, groups them into batch runs, and drives the real frame renderer: per-sprite source rects and RSXform transforms are built, then handed to a counting draw surface. `interleaved` alternates textures per sprite so every run is length 1 (worst case); `clustered` groups by texture so the run count equals the atlas count. `outline` costs nine transform passes per command by construction. `sort` measures `sortByDrawOrder` on a nearly-sorted list with K random swaps (insertion sort is O(n+k²) after k swaps).
- **Integration** — one frame = `world.step` + per-entity `coll.setPosition` + `coll.step` + `emitter.update` + sprite draw queue + `sortByDrawOrder` + `batch.flush` through the frame renderer + `endFrame`. Steady state: 300 particles + N entities (Pos+Vel + AABB collider + sprite), wrapping at the field edge so contact density does not decay while being measured. Closer shape match to a real demo frame than per-system microbenches.

## Gating native (C++) acceleration

Priority order and the standing gate decision live in [native-acceleration.md](../design/native-acceleration.md). Numbers above are the JS baseline against which any native port must demonstrate speedup.
